idiom_name: small consumer-side interfaces, internal/ packages, and syscall.Credential for child processes
implementation_notes: Go's authority story is structural and process-level. Structurally, accept the smallest interface a function needs (one or two methods) and keep implementation types unexported, so a package cannot name authority it was never handed; and use internal packages, which the go command enforces - a package under a directory named internal can only be imported from the tree rooted at the parent of internal, which is the build system acting as an authority boundary rather than a convention. For processes, exec.Cmd.SysProcAttr carries a syscall.Credential (Uid, Gid, Groups, NoSetGroups) so a child starts with exactly the identity its job needs, and the x/sys/unix package exposes the Linux capability and seccomp calls when the job needs one kernel privilege rather than a different uid. What replaces a rights table is the interface set plus the package graph; keep the classic form only where authority is genuinely dynamic (a plugin host), and then give the plugin its own process and credentials rather than a shared one.
pitfalls: A zero Credential does not mean no privileges: Uid 0 is root, so a Credential built from configuration or left unset can hand the child more than the job needs - treat it as a reviewed grant, and remember the parent keeps its own authority either way.

Interface narrowing is compile-time advice: reflection, unsafe and exported fields bypass it, and a plugin or goroutine running in-process shares the whole process's authority, including its open descriptors and environment.
internal packages are a build-time visibility rule, not a runtime boundary: code that can be linked in can be reached, so use them to keep components honest, not to contain code you do not trust.
